newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-AGE BEATS YOUTH AT FINALS, SAY MALONE, JORDAN.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-AGE BEATS YOUTH AT FINALS, SAY MALONE, JORDAN.

text.p: Generation X is at home watching, and the old guys are still playing in the NBA Finals. That's no accident, say Karl Malone, Michael Jordan or John Stockton.
Malone, 34 next month and a 12-year veteran, does not bother to hide his disdain for the idea that it is time for the old guard to gracefully hand over the NBA to the brash newcomers.
"I think it started at the All-Star game," the star power forward for the Utah Jazz said Monday. "They were saying, 'Out with the old, in with the new.'
"Like I said, a lot of them new ones are home now watching a lot of us old ones," he said, drawing laughs from a roomful of reporters on an offday ahead of Wednesday's Game 5.

"I've had young guys tell me at scorer's table, 'Hey, old man,' or 'Grandpa' or 'You all leave this game for us young guys.' And I don't know, some of these young guys, would you like to be talking to them right now?
"Probably half of them would be late," he said, again sending the room into hilarity.
"You wouldn't have enough chairs up here for all their entourage," he added, bringing down the house.

Jordan, 34 years old and a 12-year veteran as well as a four-time NBA and nine-time scoring champion for the Chicago Bulls, said it was no accident the oldies but goodies were the ones still playing in June.
"I wouldn't say it's rare," said Jordan. "You know, seven years ago I wasn't in the Finals, Karl wasn't in the Finals, Charles (Barkley) wasn't in the Finals, Scottie (Pippen) wasn't in the Finals.

"It's a sense of maturity over time, game elevating. It's a learning process that a lot of young players don't know what it feels like to be in a situation like this. We all had to take our turn to be in a situation like this.
"I know there are a lot of expectations on some of the young players expected to be great players, but they're not players enough to get their teams to this level, not at this particular time."
But the day will come for the Shaquille O'Neals and Anfernee (Penny) Hardaways, Jordan predicted.

"Shaq, some of these young players, Penny, other players who are going to work their way up to this point, they're going to take the light that's been passed on to us from Magic Johnson, Larry Bird and some of those other players."

Last year, some people felt the torch has passed to the younger Seattle SuperSonics of Gary Payton and Shawn Kemp when they won the Western Conference. Some said the old Jazz players had let time pass them by without ever reaching a Finals.

"In this business people write you off long before you say to yourself, hey, it's time," said Malone. "And hopefully I'll know when it's time. I don't want to stay one year too long, and it's the same with Stock (teammate John Stockton)."
The league's Most Valuable Player added: "I think what we said was, even though we're considered old in basketball terms, we still think we have games left."

Better games, as far as the 35-year-old Stockton is concerned: "I don't think of age as a hindrance. There's a lot of old guys in this series right here and I don't think any of us maybe can do things physically exactly the way we could do it 10 years ago.

"But there's other things you gain with the experience. Hopefully, you don't put yourself in the position where you have to use the same speed or the same jumping ability or whatever. And you learn to actually become a better player when you might not have a lot of the physical skills to work with.
"So that doesn't bug me."
The slight, unassuming Stockton, a 13-year NBA veteran with all the subtle skills of a premier point guard, especially is underestimated by young people, Malone said.

When he goes back to his native Louisiana in the summer, Malone said, "You always have some guys come up to you and say, 'You know what, I think I can take that John Stockton, you know what, he's wearing my uniform.'
"And I say to myself, 'Son, little do you know you have a tiger by the tail when you get out there on the court with him.'
"Because as friendly and as nice as he is away from the game, he can turn it on at the drop of a hat, and get ready to play."
